title: Program Logic and Decision Design
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of program logic and decision design and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply boolean conditions in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Program Logic and Decision Design is part of Conditions, Loops, and Control Flow. Start with boolean conditions and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: Control flow should make the decision rule, stopping condition and boundary behavior visible.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Control flow should make the decision rule, stopping condition and boundary behavior visible. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

items.title: Boolean Conditions
items.text: Explain boolean conditions in the context of program logic and decision design, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Handling Empty and Missing Inputs
items.text: For handling empty and missing inputs, include a failing or boundary case and explain how it should be detected without silently losing information.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Trace one ordinary case and one boundary case; for loops, verify that the loop can terminate. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Program Logic and Decision Design
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 57: Program Logic and Decision Design
example_score <- 30
if (example_score >= 50) "review" else "retry"

content_blocks.limitations: Test both sides of the branch condition and decide how missing inputs should be handled. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For program logic and decision design, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

content.task: Apply program logic and decision design to a small synthetic example. Start with boolean conditions, predict the result, compare it with a local R run, test one edge or failure case, and document one limitation. For integrations or package-dependent topics, submit a safe verification plan rather than claiming the code ran.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the boolean conditions idea in a minimal example or safe design sketch.
State the expected result before running the example.
Verify one relevant boundary, missing-value or failure case.
Record assumptions and one limitation of the result.
content.expected_output: A reproducible program logic and decision design example or design sketch with the expected result, one checked edge or failure case, and a stated limitation.
hints: Start with “Boolean Conditions” and identify the input and output before coding.
Inspect the type and shape of the result, then test one ordinary and one boundary input.
Test a boundary, missing, invalid or failure input relevant to this topic.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
